title: Teach what you know
tomorrow: Saba's old Chumash is full of pencil notes. who writes in a holy book?

segments.voice: Yesterday, learning came home: a question at dinner, a story at bedtime. Family learning. Today it takes one more step, out of your head and into someone else's.
screen: `FAMILY LEARNING.` → `OUT OF YOUR HEAD, INTO SOMEONE ELSE'S.`

segments.voice: The kitchen table, late. A younger cousin, a printout of his bar mitzvah portion, and a phone leaning on the fruit bowl, playing a recording he's supposed to copy. He looks up. You did this, right? Can you just teach me? The honest answer is: sort of. You did it once. Some of it stuck. The Talmud tells about a teacher whose student needed every lesson said again and again. And one day, even that wasn't enough.
screen: `THE KITCHEN TABLE, LATE.` → `CAN YOU JUST TEACH ME?` → `ONE DAY, IT WASN'T ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: The teacher is Rabbi Preida, in the tractate Eruvin. His student learned each lesson only after hearing it four hundred times, so Rabbi Preida said it four hundred times. One day he was needed somewhere else, for a good deed. He taught the lesson four hundred times, and the student didn't get it. What's different today? he asked. The student said: since they called you, my mind's been on the door, waiting for you to leave. So the rabbi said: pay attention. And he taught it four hundred times more. The Talmud says a voice from heaven then offered him a choice of rewards, and he chose the one his whole generation could share. Pirkei Avot puts the idea in one line. Rabbi Ishmael, son of Rabbi Yose, says: one who learns in order to teach is given the means both to learn and to teach. Teaching isn't the prize at the end of learning. It's how learning finishes. Rabbi Chanina says it from the other side, in the Talmud: much I learned from my teachers, more from my friends, and from my students most of all. Something to tell a friend tonight: in that story, the lesson is the teacher's patience, not the student's speed. You don't need to know everything to teach. You need one thing you know, and the patience to say it again.
screen: `FOUR HUNDRED TIMES.` · `A MIND ON THE DOOR.` · `LEARN IN ORDER TO TEACH.` · `FROM MY STUDENTS, MOST OF ALL.` · then, large: `TEACH IT.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing you really know: a blessing, a family recipe, a story from these lessons, how to fix a bike chain. Quietly, out loud, explain it to someone who isn't there, as simply as you can. Where you stumble is the part you're still learning.
screen: `ONE THING YOU KNOW.` · `SAY IT OUT LOUD.` · `WHERE YOU STUMBLE.`

segments.voice: Teach what you know: Rabbi Ishmael's line, lived. You learn in order to teach, and the teaching finishes the learning.
Your line: teach it. Rabbi Preida said it four hundred times more. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1751 COUNTS.` → `STUDY FOR LIFE · 9 OF 15.` → `TOMORROW: WHO WRITES NOTES IN A HOLY BOOK?`

howItsDone: In Jewish study, learners often take turns explaining a text to a partner, and a bar or bat mitzvah student may be tutored by a teacher, an older student or a relative.

match.prompt: who said what about teaching — tap the pairs.
pairs: taught it four hundred times more
had his mind on the door

myth: you have to be an expert before you can teach
Avot ties teaching to learning: one who learns in order to teach is given the means to do both.
in the Talmud story, the student finally learned because the teacher went faster
he went the other way: he asked what was different that day, then taught it four hundred times more.
a sage in the Talmud says he learned most from his students
Rabbi Chanina: much from my teachers, more from my friends, most from my students.

fork.setup: a kid you're tutoring keeps missing the same line. you've gone over it again and again, and you're running late. what would Rabbi Preida do?
options: ask what's pulling his mind away, then go over it again.
send him the recording; he'll learn faster on his own.
tell him it's fine to skip that line on the big day.
fork.reveal: Rabbi Preida asked what was different that day, learned the student was watching the door, and taught it four hundred times more.

original.note: Hebrew: to teach. Avot's phrase is ha-lomed al menat lelamed: one who learns in order to teach.

trapdoor: what you thought: you start teaching once you've finished learning.
what it means: teaching is part of learning; one who learns in order to teach is given the means to do both.
what a scholar hears: Avot 4:5 (4:6 in some editions), Rabbi Ishmael son of Rabbi Yose; Rabbi Preida in Eruvin 54b; Rabbi Chanina in Taanit 7a.
guess: passing on what you've learned, which finishes the learning
waiting to teach until you've mastered the whole text
leaving all teaching to rabbis and trained teachers
recall: a question at dinner, a story at bedtime

chat.says: ok new thing. aunt dana wants me to tutor eli for his bar mitzvah. i barely remember mine??
options: Say yes. Teaching is part of learning; you'll relearn yours while you teach his.
Say no. Only teach what you've fully mastered, the way a rabbi would.
Send him the recording instead. Teaching is the rabbi's job, not a cousin's.
chat.meaning: Avot says one who learns in order to teach is given the means to learn and to teach. You don't need to be an expert first.

bar mitzvah.meaning: a Jewish boy's coming of age, often marked by reading Torah

Talmud.meaning: the great collection of rabbinic discussion built on the Mishnah

Rabbi Preida.meaning: a sage the Talmud remembers for his patience as a teacher

Pirkei Avot.meaning: a book of the Mishnah collecting the sages' sayings

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 4:5 (4:6 in some editions): Rabbi Ishmael son of Rabbi Yose, one who learns in order to teach is given the means to learn and to teach
Babylonian Talmud, Eruvin 54b (Rabbi Preida and his student)
Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 7a (Rabbi Chanina: from my students most of all)

notes: Avot 4:5 paraphrased; the saying's number differs by edition (4:5 or 4:6). Confirm attribution to Rabbi Ishmael son of Rabbi Yose.

Eruvin 54b paraphrased: Rabbi Preida taught a student each lesson four hundred times; when called away for a mitzvah the student was distracted and he taught it four hundred times more; a heavenly voice offered a choice of reward (added years, or the World to Come for him and his generation) and he chose the latter. Simplified as 'a choice of rewards ... the one his whole generation could share.' Confirm.
Taanit 7a, Rabbi Chanina (teachers, colleagues, students) paraphrased. Confirm.
Surprising fact: in the Preida story the lesson is the teacher's patience, not the student's speed (Eruvin 54b).
